written.myAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water from the aerial parts of a plant in the form of water vapour. Its types are stomatal, cuticular and lenticular transpiration.

Transpiration is the loss of water as water vapour, mainly through stomata and mostly during the day. Guttation is the release of liquid water droplets through pores at leaf tips or edges, usually at night.
Rubber plants excrete latex, while keekar (Acacia) trees excrete gums through special pores.

Plants lose excess water by transpiration and, in some plants, by guttation. Dissolved salts and other wastes may be stored in leaves or as crystals; wastes in leaves are removed when the leaves fall.

During the day, carbon dioxide produced in respiration is used in photosynthesis, and some oxygen produced by photosynthesis is used in respiration. Excess oxygen is released through stomata. At night, photosynthesis stops, so excess carbon dioxide is released through general surfaces and stomata.

Plants release excess carbon dioxide through general surfaces and stomata, and excess oxygen through stomata. They remove extra water by transpiration and, in some plants, by guttation. Other wastes may be stored as harmless crystals or in leaves that later fall, or excreted through special pores. Examples include latex from rubber plants, gums from Acacia (keekar) trees, resins from conifers, and mucilage from ladyfinger.
